prompt: How many squares are on a standard chessboard?
rationale: The standard board is eight squares by eight squares.

prompt: How many pieces does each player have at the start of a standard chess game?
rationale: Each side starts with eight pawns and eight other pieces.

prompt: How many pawns does each player start with in standard chess?
rationale: The second rank for each player is occupied by eight pawns.

prompt: Which chess piece moves any number of unobstructed squares along a rank or file, but not diagonally?
rationale: Rooks move horizontally or vertically; the obstruction qualification matters.

prompt: Which chess piece makes the familiar L-shaped move?
rationale: A knight moves two squares along one axis and one along the other.

prompt: Which chess piece can jump over intervening pieces during its ordinary move?
rationale: Knights can jump; ordinary rook, bishop and queen moves cannot pass through pieces.

prompt: Apart from castling, how far may a king move in one standard chess move?
answers: Two squares in a straight line
rationale: The king normally moves to an adjacent legal square.

prompt: In chess, may you make a move that leaves your own king under attack?
answers: Yes, whenever you capture a pawn
Yes, if your queen is safe
Yes, but only on your first turn
rationale: A move leaving the moving player king in check is illegal.

prompt: What is the result when a player checkmates the opposing king in standard chess?
answers: Both kings are removed and play continues
The losing player gets another move
rationale: Checkmate ends the game with a win, rather than requiring capture of the king.

prompt: In an ordinary chess capture, which way does a pawn take an opposing piece?
rationale: Ordinary pawn captures are one diagonal square forwards; en passant has special conditions.

prompt: How does a chess pawn normally advance when it is not capturing?
rationale: Pawn non-capturing movement is forwards, with a possible initial two-square move.

prompt: What happens when a chess pawn legally reaches the farthest rank?
answers: It is promoted to another permitted piece
It returns to its starting square
rationale: Promotion replaces it with a queen, rook, bishop or knight of the same colour.

prompt: At the start of standard chess, the white queen stands on a square of which colour?
answers: Either colour chosen by its player
rationale: The queen begins on her own colour: white queen on d1.

prompt: When setting up a standard chessboard, what colour is the nearest corner square on your right?
rationale: The near right corner must be a light square.

prompt: In ordinary chess tournament scoring, how many points does each player receive for a draw?
rationale: The usual win/draw/loss scores are 1, half and 0; special scoring systems are excluded by ordinary.

prompt: Which letter represents the king in English algebraic chess notation?
rationale: English notation uses K for king; N is knight.

prompt: Which letter represents the queen in English algebraic chess notation?
rationale: English algebraic notation uses Q for queen.

prompt: In algebraic chess notation, the numbers 1 to 8 identify what?
rationale: Ranks are numbered; files are lettered a to h.

prompt: In algebraic chess notation, the letters a to h identify what?
rationale: The eight vertical files use lowercase letters.

prompt: What is a chess clock mainly used to track?
answers: The thinking time available to each player
rationale: A chess clock tracks the players allotted time, not simply the number of moves.

prompt: How many suits are in a standard French-suited pack of playing cards?
rationale: The suits are hearts, diamonds, clubs and spades.

prompt: Which pair of suits is red in a standard French-suited pack?
rationale: Hearts and diamonds are red; clubs and spades are black.

prompt: Excluding jokers, how many cards are in a standard French-suited pack?
rationale: Four suits with thirteen ranks give fifty-two cards; jokers are excluded.

prompt: Which group contains the three face-card ranks in a standard French-suited pack?
rationale: The illustrated court/face cards are jack, queen and king.

prompt: How many aces are in a standard 52-card pack?
rationale: There is one ace in each of the four suits.

prompt: What does shuffling a pack of cards do?
answers: Mixes up the order of the cards
Sorts every card into numerical order
Removes all jokers from the pack
rationale: Shuffling rearranges the pack before play; it does not alter card identities.

prompt: In a card game, what does dealing mean?
answers: Mixing the order of the pack
Placing a held card on the discard pile
rationale: Dealing distributes the cards, commonly one or a few at a time.

prompt: In card-game terminology, what is a player's hand?
answers: The cards that player currently holds
rationale: A hand can also mean a round; the player possessive makes the held-card meaning clear.

prompt: What does it mean to discard a card during play?
answers: Put it aside as the rules allow
Take a new card into your hand
Mix the order of the entire pack
Deal a new hand to every player
rationale: Discarding removes a card from the held cards to the designated discard area.

prompt: In card games, what does drawing a card normally mean?
answers: Taking a card from an available pile or source
Putting a held card on the discard pile
Spreading your entire hand face up
Mixing the order of the pack
rationale: Draw means take a card under the rules; it need not always come from the stock.

prompt: In a trick-taking card game, what is a trick?
answers: A round in which players each contribute a card
The full pack before it is dealt
The total score for one player
The face-down cards not yet dealt
rationale: A trick is the set of cards played in a round, usually one per player.

prompt: In many trick-taking games, what special advantage does the trump suit have?
answers: It can beat cards from other suits
Every card in it is worth zero
It is removed before every deal
rationale: Trumps outrank nontrumps within the game rules; the question does not override obligations to follow suit.

prompt: In card games, what does following suit mean?
answers: Playing a card of the suit that was led
Playing the same numerical rank regardless of suit
rationale: Follow suit refers to the suit led, not to matching rank.

prompt: Who distributes the cards at the start of a hand in a conventional card game?
answers: The person holding the most aces
The previous winner in every game
rationale: Dealer is the role distributing cards; how the role is selected varies.

prompt: How many players take part in a standard game of contract bridge?
rationale: Contract bridge is played by four players in two partnerships.

prompt: In contract bridge, where does your partner sit?
rationale: The partners occupy opposite seats, conventionally North/South and East/West.

prompt: Which of these is traditionally a trick-taking card game?
rationale: Whist is trick taking; the alternatives are matching, solitaire and melding games.

prompt: In the card game Snap, what match are players normally watching for?
rationale: Ordinary Snap matches ranks; illustration-based children decks may use matching pictures.

prompt: Which term commonly describes a card game intended for one person?
rationale: Patience/solitaire describes single-player card games rather than two-team play.

prompt: In traditional Rummy, which cards form a run?
answers: Consecutive ranks in the same suit
Three cards of the same rank
One card from each of four suits
A king, seven and two of mixed suits
rationale: A run is a same-suit sequence; a set uses equal ranks.

prompt: In Blackjack, which total are players trying to approach without exceeding it?
rationale: The target is twenty-one; exceeding it is a bust.

prompt: What does bust mean in Blackjack?
answers: The hand contains exactly two cards
The dealer has shuffled the cards
rationale: Bust describes a total over twenty-one, not an ordinary initial hand.

prompt: In standard five-card poker, what is a flush?
answers: Five cards of the same suit, not all in sequence
Five consecutive ranks of mixed suits
Two pairs and an unmatched card
Three matching-rank cards and two other ranks
rationale: A flush shares a suit; a straight flush is a stronger special case.

prompt: In standard five-card poker, what is a straight?
answers: Five consecutive ranks, not all of the same suit
Five cards of one suit with nonconsecutive ranks
Two pairs and an unmatched card
Four cards of the same rank and a fifth card
rationale: A straight uses consecutive ranks; it need not share a suit.

prompt: In poker, what does one pair mean?
answers: Two cards of the same rank
Two cards of the same suit only
rationale: Pair refers to matching rank, not just suit or consecutive values.

prompt: In standard poker, three of a kind means three cards sharing what?
rationale: Three of a kind means a matched rank, such as three sevens.

prompt: In standard poker, four of a kind contains how many cards of the same rank?
rationale: Four matching ranks are possible because the standard pack has four suits.

prompt: Which cards form a royal flush in standard five-card poker?
answers: Ten, jack, queen, king and ace of one suit
Five through nine of one suit
rationale: The royal flush is the ace-high straight flush.

prompt: In poker, what does bluffing involve?
answers: Trying to make opponents believe your hand is stronger than it is
Removing every low card from the pack
rationale: Bluffing represents strength to influence opponents despite lacking the represented hand.

prompt: What does folding mean in a poker hand?
answers: Giving up that hand rather than continuing
Continuing without adding a bet when permitted
rationale: Folding relinquishes further participation in the current hand.

prompt: How many men does each side start with in English draughts?
rationale: English draughts uses twelve men per side on an eight-by-eight board.

prompt: In English draughts, which squares are used for play?
rationale: The men are placed and moved on the dark squares.

prompt: In English draughts, how does an ordinary uncrowned man make a non-capturing move?
rationale: Uncrowned men make ordinary moves one vacant diagonal square forwards.

prompt: In English draughts, how is an opposing piece captured?
answers: By jumping over it to an empty square beyond
By landing on top of it
By moving beside it without jumping
By surrounding it with four pieces
rationale: A capturing jump passes over the adjacent opponent and removes it.

prompt: In English draughts, what does a man become when it reaches the farthest row?
answers: A pawn of the opposite colour
rationale: Reaching the king row crowns the man.

prompt: Which extra direction can a king move in English draughts compared with an ordinary man?
rationale: A crowned king can move and capture diagonally backwards as well as forwards.

prompt: In English draughts, what happens if the player whose turn it is has no legal move?
answers: The board is rotated and play restarts
rationale: A player with no legal move loses, whether blocked or without pieces.

prompt: In traditional Snakes and Ladders, what happens when your piece lands on the head of a snake?
answers: It moves down to the tail
It moves up to the highest square
It changes to another player's colour
It is removed for the rest of the game
rationale: Landing at the snake head sends the counter down its body to the tail.

prompt: In traditional Snakes and Ladders, what happens when your piece lands at the foot of a ladder?
answers: It climbs to the top of that ladder
It moves backwards to the start
It changes direction for the rest of the game
It swaps places with every other piece
rationale: A ladder takes the counter from its lower end to its upper end.

prompt: In Snakes and Ladders, movement is determined mainly by what?
answers: Chance from a die or spinner
The number of cards in your hand
Your ability to spell a long word
rationale: Random movement rather than player-chosen tactical moves drives the race.

prompt: What is the usual objective in Ludo?
answers: Get all your pieces around the track and home
rationale: Ludo is a race to bring the player pieces home.

prompt: In classic Ludo, what normally happens to an opponent's lone piece when you land on its unprotected square?
answers: It goes back to its starting area
It swaps colours with your piece
rationale: Landing on an opposing single counter sends that counter back to its starting area. Protected spaces and blocks have additional rules.

prompt: How many playing pieces does each player normally have in classic Ludo?
rationale: The familiar classic game gives each colour four counters.

prompt: What usually marks the two halves of a traditional domino tile?
rationale: Traditional dominoes show pips on two ends; blank ends represent zero.

prompt: In dominoes, what is a double?
answers: A tile with the same number at both ends
Two players taking a turn together
A tile with a letter at one end

prompt: How many tiles are in a standard double-six domino set?

prompt: In a simple matching domino game, what must the touching ends of adjoining tiles show?

prompt: How many matching symbols in a straight line win an ordinary game of noughts and crosses?

prompt: What is the size of the grid in ordinary noughts and crosses?

prompt: In Nine Men's Morris, what is a line of three of your pieces called?

prompt: Which objects are traditionally moved between pits in mancala games?

prompt: What shape is the familiar Chinese checkers board?

A plain circle with one central hole

prompt: What are traditionally moved along a scoring board to keep score in Cribbage?
rationale: Cribbage uses pegs in board holes to record the running score.

By bidding a number of points
By spelling a word from tiles

prompt: In Pictionary, how does a player normally communicate the clue to teammates?

prompt: What do players collect in their circular playing token in classic Trivial Pursuit?

prompt: In Boggle, what do players try to find in the grid of lettered cubes?

Only in a single straight vertical line
